claims.head: Who drives the play: the Bruins
claims.body: The Bruins have been near the top of the league at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Maple Leafs one of the worst. Expect the Bruins to spend more of the night in the Maple Leafs’ end. That’s about the puck, not the scoreboard: goalies and finishing decide plenty of games the chances don’t.

claims.head: Patience vs. spray-and-pray
claims.body: On shot quality, Boston is one of the league’s best, but Toronto is one of the worst. They’re about as far apart as two teams get. The more dangerous chances are likely to be the Bruins’.

notes.text: Kirill Marchenko has not dressed for the last 12 games. He is one of their most valuable skaters.

Nick Blankenburg is on injured reserve (upper-body injury) and has missed the last 14 games. He is one of their more valuable skaters. Troy Stecher has taken his spot beside Oliver Ekman-Larsson. That pair has had 51% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 73:06 together, about what it had with Blankenburg (48%).
Jack Roslovic is out (upper-body injury) and missed their last game. He is a top-six forward. Nick Paul has taken his spot beside Auston Matthews and Easton Cowan.
Kirill Marchenko is expected back after missing 12 games. Their recent numbers were built mostly without him.
Aatu Räty was added to the roster on Nov 23 and has played beside William Nylander and Dakota Joshua.
Oliver Ekman-Larsson has started killing penalties: on the ice for 31% of the team’s shorthanded time in 25 games, up from 6% last season.

James Hagens is day to day and has missed the last 7 games. Marat Khusnutdinov has taken his spot beside Elias Lindholm and Casey Mittelstadt. That line has had 67% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 34:16 together, up from 54% with Hagens.

stakes: The Maple Leafs go in tied for seventh in the Atlantic with 21 points, 10 points behind the Bruins, tied for fourth.

story.head: Who drives the play: the Bruins
paras: The Maple Leafs (9-14-3) beat the Islanders 4-2 on Monday, while the Bruins (15-8-1) lost 4-2 to Winnipeg on Wednesday. This is an Atlantic Division matchup, with the Maple Leafs last (tied for 26th in the NHL) and the Bruins fourth (tied for tenth).

The Maple Leafs have played better than their record (.404) says: their chances are worth about .490, mostly because they’re 3-10 in one-goal games. The Bruins’ record (.646) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.573), largely thanks to their goaltending.

The Maple Leafs get their shots through better than anyone (1st), but have had shaky goaltending (31st). The Bruins, by contrast, have had some of the best goaltending in the league (2nd). The Leafs also take a lot of low-quality shots (31st), so the Bruins wait for good looks, but they settle for hopeful ones. On the other side, the Bruins leave the shooting to their forwards (2nd lowest) and sit back rather than chase on the forecheck (2nd lowest). Boston has allowed 2.71 goals a game, the fourth fewest in the league. The Maple Leafs’ knack for getting shots through meets the Bruins’ shot blockers.

Auston Matthews (14 G / 20 A / 34 P in 26 GP) leads the Maple Leafs in scoring and is tied for sixth in the NHL, and William Nylander (11 G / 14 A / 25 P in 26 GP) isn’t far behind. For the Bruins, David Pastrňák (11 G / 21 A / 32 P in 24 GP) leads the way in scoring, with eight points in his last five games and a point in five straight games against Toronto.
Anthony Stolarz (6-5-1 / .902 SV% in 12 GS) is expected to start for Toronto, and Jeremy Swayman (11-6-1 / .901 SV% in 18 GS) for Boston.
The Bruins usually control more of the chances than the Maple Leafs do.
